newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Thai Central Bank sees lower growth, rates.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thai Central Bank sees lower growth, rates.

text.p: The Thai central bank on Monday scaled back its economic growth projection for 1997, but said the nation's sharply slowing economy could begin a gradual recovery soon.

The Bank of Thailand also said on Monday it saw room for Thai lending rates to ease soon, which would help spur an economy estimated to expand by less than six percent -- its slowest pace in 10 years. Central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond told a press conference he expected Thai gross domestic product to grow 5.9 percent in 1997 against 7.1 percent projected at the start of the year and a 6.4 percent expansion a year ago.
"The slowing economy in the first quarter changed the outlook for the whole year from what we had projected earlier," he said.
The governor said the projected slower growth could be attributed partly to persistent weak exports and government budget cuts this year and in the 1997/1998 (October/September) fiscal year.

Rerngchai said sluggish exports, which contracted 0.2 percent in 1996, rose only 1.5 percent during the first quarter of 1997. He said exports for the whole of 1997 should increase 7.2 percent, a downward revision of an earlier 7.7-percent projection. The Thai economy was riding high during the first half of the 1990s, with exports growing more than 20 percent a year. But the economy has been h it by an export slowdown, high interest rates that stifle business activity, tight liquidity, a stock market at eight-year-lows and a depressed property sector. Rerngchai's deputy Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi said this weakening of key economic indicators should bottom out by mid-1997 or early in the third quarter then enter a gradual recovery phase.

The governor and other officials said that while the central bank would maintain its prudent monetary policies, it expected commercial banks to cut lending rates soon to give businesses access to cheaper funding. The Bank of Thailand on Monday adjusted the guidelines it sets for commercial banks in fixing retail lending rates, which it said would open the way for banks to reduce interest rates and make them more reflective of market liquidity.

Referring to its decision early this month to adopt a two-tier baht/dollar exchange rate system to counter market speculation against the currency, a central bank statement said the authorities would take steps to ensure that the measure would not hurt funding of domestic business and investment.

Thailand has blocked access for foreign hedge funds to tap short-term baht to finance their attacks on the currency. The central bank has asked Thai-based banks to quote baht swaps at exorbitant annualised rates of about 1,000 percent.

Rerngchai said the economy had stabilised during the first quarter, with inflation easing and the current-account deficit narrowing. The Bank of Thailand on Monday said inflation would likely fall to 4.5 percent in 1997 against 5.8 percent projected earlier. Inflation was 5.8 percent in 1996. Rerngchai said, however, that the current slowdown might not end soon due to gluts in industrial capac ity and the property sector. He said private investment growth, which has steadily declined since 1995, would likely fall to only two percent this year against 7.4 percent projected earlier in 1997 and against 4.8 percent growth a year ago.
Outstanding bank credits would also increase at a sluggish 12.5 percent this year against 14.2 percent in 1996 and 24.2 percent a year earlier.
The governor also confirmed market expectations that the government would end the 1996/1997 fiscal year with a projected 23.1 billion baht budget deficit, its first in 10 years.
